items.title: Show HN: Nodecode, open-source living agent in Lisp that rewrites itself for you
items.summary: Hi HN, we're Mike and Thom. Agents of the future should only have one tool (the interpreter, ideally a LISP eval), nothing more or less; to interact with the world. Agents remember by writing markdown files. NODECODE remembers by rewriting itself. And that is in itself a new paradigm in working with agents. What if memories, skills, MCPs, provider connectors, tools, etc. all live under the same image as *.lisp files instead of in disarray across random folders? Ask it for something it can’t do, and it writes what it needs into its OWN running image and keeps it even after a restart. (Changes in a LISP image have significantly lower ceremony and overhead than in harnesses written in other languages): Small intuitive scenario: > you can't read PDFs. teach yourself. (defun read-pdf (path) ...) ; runs at once, kept (read-pdf "invoices/0421.pdf") ;; Globex owes $1,240.00, due Oct 24, unpaid. [… rest of PDF content] read-pdf is still there after a restart, in your terminal, and in every other UI clients (Discord, web app, etc.) Technically at a lower level; NODECODE runs as one process in SBCL, a Common Lisp system, and shells attach to it. The model has one tool: it evaluates LISP in the running program. Code is data, so a program can rewrite itself while it runs. What the model defines runs at once and is kept, one file per definition, committed with git, loaded at every start. Why LISP now? Current SOTA models have reached an optimum point in how they efficiently work with LISP, though not as fluently as Python. Still, we believe AGI will understand ANY language (past/present/future) by understanding the crux of any given language, and not through excessive and expensive pretraining scheme. Why LISP in general? We believe LISP is the current language that communicates to the world with the least bandwidth. Why another LISP agent? The LISP harnesses we found are hard to use unless you already know the language itself, and so we had this idea of simplifying and condensing the UX to be user friendly for the masses, while leveraging the power of LISP. Code as data is what lets an agent change itself, and that shouldn't need a LISP hacker to run. NODECODE is our first step toward putting it on everyone's PC and mobile. You ask in plain words, the model writes LISP, and you get briefed in natural language; that is how it should be. Extensions? Code as data also suits extensions. We see NODECODE as a living agent organism. To us, it feels very much alive, and so this brings us to the Cells system. A Cell is a folder that teaches NODECODE something new: a chat room it can live in (e.g Discord, Telegram, Slack, etc. - Yes we made Cells for channels to have it act as a very capable personal agent), a skill, a memory, MCPs, new tools, etc. Install one from our Cell hub or ask it to write a custom, personalized one. Either way it is more code the agent can read and change. Your terminal, a browser tab, your phone and bots in Discord, Telegram and Slack all attach to that SAME gateway process, so a tool it writes in one is there in ALL of them. Over time it becomes yours and it is continuously evolving; the organism within it; NODECODE. MIT License. https://github.com/nodecode-ai/nodecode X/twitter/demo launch post: https://x.com/pomterree/status/2113721985167728757 docs: https://nodecode.ai/docs

items.content_excerpt: A Claude Code plugin that notices tasks you keep repeating and offers to save them as a skill you can run with /name . These screenshots come from a real Claude Code 2.1.308 session in a demo repo, after asking for the same changelog update in three sessions. 1. Create the skill. [Create /update-changelog] fills in /skill-spotter:draft p1 . Claude reads the recorded steps, then asks one question: should only you be able to start the skill, or Claude too? 2. It's saved as .claude/skills/update-changelog/SKILL.md , with the steps Claude actually took. 4. Track it. /skill-spotter:status shows what it found and whether you use the skills you created. All data stays on your machine. skill-spotter keeps one SQLite file in Claude Code's plugin data folder ( ~/.claude/plugins/data/skill-spotter-…/ ). The hooks that record your turns are plain Python with no networking code. Nothing is uploaded, and there are no analytics. When data leaves your machine. This only happens through commands you run yourself: Or try it for one session from a clone: claude --plugin-dir /path/to/skill-spotter . You need Claude Code and python3 3.9+ on your PATH (macOS's built-in one works). There's nothing to pip install . Repeated instructions. items.story_key: story|title:quill desktop lightweight ai harness no electron webkit native gui
items.content_excerpt: Download from Github releases and run. Uses portable executables so no install is required. Note: the MacOS build is unsigned because I am not spending US$99/year for an Apple developer account Quill uses the work done by the Zed editor , utilizing their cross platform gpui-kit . Simply put, gpui leverages native APIs (Metal, Vulkan and DirectX) to draw the UI. You can think of it as using a game engine to render a UI, except it only renders frames when things are moving, ensuring power usage / battery life is unaffected. It renders frames at your screen's refresh rate (e.g. 144fps) so the experience is buttery smooth. All the current desktop harnesses are built on top of Electron (basically a full-fat dedicated clone of Chrome running only one website). Conventionally, this is done to minimize the friction associated with cross-platform application development and be competitive in feature delivery. Essentially, sacrifice a little user experience in exchange for the ability to move faster than competitors. In my view, harnesses have reached a level of maturity now where the features we expect from them are well enough defined. In addition, there is no longer the pressure to be a first mover in the Desktop Agent Harness space. I think we can now afford a high quality tool that respects your computers resources while also supporting all model providers. Additionally, the technology powering Quill means that adding features is not so hard that it justifies an Electron build. I have gone with an unconventional non-commercial license that has an clause for AI training. I'm not anti-AI at all (obviously) and have no expectations that my license will be respected. The intention is that - should this code be included in training data - throw a little something my way for the training data. If you're doing research or working on an open weight model, feel free to include this in your training data. This is a weekend project of mine. If you genuinely enjoy it and want to see more, please consider starring the repo and supporting my efforts.

items.title: Beyond Final Outcomes: Quantifying Claim-Level Information Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Interaction
items.summary: When LLM-powered agents interact, information is repeatedly shared, expanded, and forgotten, yet multi-agent evaluation typically focuses on final task outcomes. We study such interaction as claim-level information dynamics and propose RIVER, which decomposes agent outputs into atomic claims and evaluates three complementary dimensions: convergence, exploration, and retention. Convergence captures cross-agent claim correspondence and stance alignment; exploration captures semantic breadth and extension beyond the source; and retention tracks source preservation and the persistence of new claims across stages and lineages. We evaluate five interaction strategies on 40 controlled news-generation cases. Repeatedly pooled interaction promotes convergence but narrows the information space, whereas distributed relay yields broader, less shared information. Further comparisons show that method-specific constraints increase exploration while weakening convergence and retention. Our findings suggest that collective information dynamics are better explained by underlying information-flow mechanisms than by simple downstream performance.

items.title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

items.title: Flownomaly: Single-Step Conditional-Mean Recovery for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
items.summary: Few-shot industrial anomaly detection requires modeling category-specific normality from only a handful of defect-free images. Common approaches tie inference to stored exemplars, impose rigid linear structure, or risk reproducing anomalous content. Flownomaly instead casts the problem as normal-counterpart recovery in frozen DINOv2 feature space. Given normal supports, a velocity field is learned through conditional flow matching over frozen patch tokens to transport Gaussian noise toward normal features. Along straight paths, a single recovery step using one evaluation of the optimal field yields the posterior mean of the clean normal token without trajectory integration. The operating time governs how strongly recovery modifies a query token. With no anomalous validation samples available for tuning, a normal-only Jacobian gain-to-noise criterion selects this time from the supports alone. Squared residuals between query tokens and their recovered counterparts yield anomaly signals for both dense localization and image-level detection. Across 1-, 2-, and 4-shot benchmarks on MVTec-AD and VisA, together with sample-shot evaluations on Real-IAD, Flownomaly achieves state-of-the-art performance against recent category-specific methods. In the 1-shot setting, image- and pixel-level AUROC reach 97.8% and 98.0% on MVTec-AD and 95.3% and 98.7% on VisA, with a 2.1-point image-level AUROC improvement over the strongest baseline on VisA. Code is available at https://github.com/b-rbmp/Flownomaly.

items.title: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
items.summary: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms.

items.title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents
items.summary: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.

items.title: vllm v0.32.0
items.summary:
v0.32.0

Highlights

This release features 814 commits from 363 contributors (121 new)!

  • Structured decisions and generic parsers: the new POST /v1/systemone endpoint answers choice, noul and score questions over a structured state (#59299), is served by default (#60677, #60696), and also runs on Cloudflare/clef-omni (#61064), LiquidAI/d1-3B (#60676) and DiffusionGemma (#60466). The new hf tool and reasoning parser (--tool-call-parser hf, --reasoning-parser hf) reads the checkpoint's response_template, so models that ship it need no model-specific parser (#58604, #58602), in both the Python and Rust frontends (#59005).
  • Low-precision KV cache everywhere: NVFP4 KV cache now runs on SM8x and SM12x (#46963), SM90 (#60620) and with XQA decode on SM12x (#60452), and on MiniMax-M3 sparse attention on SM100 (#59300); GLM-5.x defaults to an FP8 KV cache on SM100, halving KV memory per rank with 2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark (#60140, #60281); fp8_ds_mla on SM90 gives GLM-5.3-Flash up to 31% more output throughput (#59246); ROCm gains the 4-bit ultraquant_4bit KV cache with about 2x the density of FP8 (#57057).
  • Model Runner V2: a GPU n-gram speculator with variable-length drafts (#40704), Elastic EP (#53934), pipeline parallelism with prefill context parallelism for MLA models (#59139), a stock torch.compile mode (#59079), and MRV2 is now the default on ROCm with the model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360).

items.title: Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud
items.summary:
Every organization has unique requirements for building and scaling generative AI. At Google Cloud, we are committed to giving developers model choice and architectural flexibility to run workloads however they need.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

Both options deliver the same frontier models on day zero, the same pricing, and the same Google Cloud billing. The difference comes down to who acts as your data processor and whether you need access to the new Claude platform features when they launch:

[NEW] Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)

Delivers day-zero access to Claude models and Claude Platform features such as Claude Managed Agents (beta), skills, and code execution. Anthropic operates the stack as the data processor on Google Cloud infrastructure under Anthropic’s terms of service, while organizations authenticate with Google Cloud IAM, maintain Cloud Audit Logging, and consolidate spend under their existing Google Cloud billing and eligible commitments.

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic-managed).

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Continues to deliver day-zero access to the latest Claude models with strict governance, compliance, and sovereignty requirements. Google Cloud operates as the data processor under existing customer agreements, providing VPC Service Controls, Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), and data residency in the U.S., EU, and APAC. New Claude Platform features roll out over time as they are integrated into the Google-managed infrastructure. Teams also benefit from native integrations with Google Cloud services like BigQuery and Model Armor, along with standard billing and eligible commitment drawdown. 

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

No matter how you choose to deploy, you can access Anthropic's latest frontier models on Google Cloud, including Claude Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Opus 5.5, with new platform features available immediately on the Anthropic-managed option and rolling out on the Google-managed option once integrated. This gives developers the full spectrum of reasoning, coding, and multi-modal capabilities with Google Cloud IAM and Marketplace billing. Get started.
